title: Diesel Is Falling. Now Everyone Wants Their Surcharge Back: Canadian Fuel Decisions for Winter 2026-27
summary: Canadian diesel fell from a $2.75 record to about $2.46. With Alberta, PEI and federal fuel taxes returning in 2027, here's how to reset fuel surcharges.
body_markdown:
The email lands at 7:40 on a Monday. Subject line: "Fuel surcharge relief, effective immediately."


You run pricing and operations for a hybrid shop out of the GTA. Roughly 70 tractors, a brokerage desk that moves another few hundred loads a month, and lanes that run from Montreal to Calgary with a steady stream of southbound cross-border work.


The sender is your largest shipper's procurement lead. Her note is short and polite. Diesel is down, she writes. She's seen it at the pump. She'd like to see it on your invoices, starting this week.


She isn't wrong. She just isn't seeing the whole picture. And neither, it turns out, is your fuel table.


(The carrier is illustrative. The numbers are not.)


## How you got here: the fall nobody forgot


Rewind to September. You remember it the way you remember a bad storm.


Natural Resources Canada's national average for diesel hit about $2.75 a litre in mid-September 2026, far above the old record of roughly $2.25 set in 2022, according to Canadian Press reporting on the federal data. NRCan's daily table peaked at 276.7 cents on September 18.


What that meant for you: every truck burned through margin faster than any surcharge could catch it. One Canadian private-fleet association leader told reporters at the end of September that a round-trip Montreal-Toronto haul that cost roughly $850 on January 1 was running about $1,400.


The cause wasn't mainly crude. It was refining. A national fuel-price survey found the diesel refining margin hit an all-time high of 142.2 cents a litre on September 21, more than half the pump price. Middle East shipping disruptions and damaged Russian refining capacity had drained global diesel stocks just as harvest and heating demand arrived.


That matters now because refining margins don't fall on a schedule. They fall when inventories rebuild, and that can reverse in a week.


So when your shipper says "diesel is down," you need to know exactly how far, and where.


## Monday, 8:15 a.m.: the number she's looking at


You pull the federal data before you reply.


NRCan's national average was $2.456 a litre for the week reported November 23. That's roughly 10% below the September record, and about 18 cents below October's monthly average of 263.4 cents.


So yes, she has a point. A drop of 18 cents a litre is real money. At 40 litres per 100 kilometres (my illustration, not a fleet benchmark), it's about 7 cents a kilometre, or about $70 on a 1,000 km lane.


But look closer at what's still embedded in the price.


In Vancouver, NRCan's weekly average was 254.7 cents a litre for the week ending November 24. That's 45 cents off the year's peak. It's also still 73 cents above the same week in 2025. NRCan's estimate of the refining margin in that price was 138.8 cents, against 86.6 cents a year earlier.


What that means for you: diesel is falling from a cliff, not returning to normal. Anyone pricing as if $1.80 diesel is around the corner is pricing a hope.


That's the first thing you'll put in your reply. The second is harder, because it's about your own table.


## 9:00 a.m.: your table is lying to both of you


Your fuel surcharge schedule was built three years ago. It pegs to the national average, updates monthly from the prior month's figure, and uses a base price nobody in the building can explain.


Here's what that does in a falling market.


Your November surcharge is calculated off October's average. October was the most expensive month of the year. So right now, your invoices are collecting fuel at roughly 263 cents while your trucks buy closer to 246.


For a few weeks, that gap is your friend. It's also exactly why the shipper's email exists. She sees the pump price. She sees your surcharge. They don't match, and the gap runs in your favour.


The same lag nearly broke you in September. Ontario's weekly survey jumped about 16 cents a litre in a single week that month. A monthly surcharge was weeks behind. You ate it.


That's the real lesson of this fall: a lagging table isn't neutral. It's a bet on direction, and you placed it without deciding to.


Then there's the index itself. Diesel isn't one price in Canada. A trade publication reviewed one small fleet's fuel-card list for November 11: $1.91 a litre in Edmonton, $2.21 in Brampton, $2.54 in Laval. On a 1,000-litre fill, Laval costs about $625 more than Edmonton.


What that means for you: a national-average surcharge overpays you on western lanes and underpays you in Quebec. Your shipper's eastern freight may actually be underpriced, while her Alberta freight is carrying it.


So before you answer her, you need to know which lanes you're defending and which ones you're quietly winning.


## 10:30 a.m.: the tax calendar nobody priced


Here's the part your shipper hasn't seen, and the part most rate cards ignore. A chunk of today's lower price is temporary tax relief, and it starts expiring in five weeks.


Start out west. Alberta paused its 13-cent provincial fuel tax on October 1, 2026, after its quarterly oil-price review came in above the $90 trigger. The province says the pause runs until at least December 31, and the earliest it would restart collection is January 1, 2027. When it comes back, it can rise by no more than 9 cents a litre per quarter.


What it means in practice: a western lane priced off today's Edmonton pump could see as much as 9 cents of tax return on New Year's Day, then more the following quarter, depending on oil.


Prince Edward Island set its 14.15-cent diesel tax to zero from September 26, 2026 through January 31, 2027, according to the province's regulator. That one has a hard date.


Then the federal layer. Ottawa suspended its 4-cent excise tax on diesel on April 20, 2026. Legislation that received Royal Assent on October 29 extends the suspension to January 31, 2027. After that, it returns at 2 cents from February 1 and the full 4 cents on April 1.


None of these are huge on their own. Stacked, they add up. And because sales tax applies on top, each step is slightly bigger at the pump than the headline number.


Now remember who pays where. Under IFTA, fuel tax is owed in the province where the kilometres are driven, not where the fuel was bought. Fill up cheaply in Alberta and run through Quebec, and you still owe Quebec's tax on those kilometres on your quarterly return.


What it means for you: cheap western fuel is partly an illusion for interprovincial fleets. The pre-tax gap is real savings. The tax gap comes back as a bill.


So the honest answer to "diesel is down" is: yes, and some of that drop has an expiry date your contract doesn't mention.


## 11:45 a.m.: the brokerage desk has its own problem


Your brokerage lead walks over with a different version of the same email.


His carriers want their fuel protected. Your customers want theirs passed back. Half of his loads run on all-in rates, where fuel is buried inside a single number. The other half split linehaul and fuel, but the carrier's surcharge and the customer's surcharge use different indexes and different update days.


In September, that mismatch cost him. Carriers repriced weekly; customers paid monthly. In November, it's flipped, and he's quietly earning margin he can't explain line by line.


That's fine until a customer audits. Then it looks like he's padding fuel.


The market isn't making it easier. A Canadian load board's October data showed spot volumes up 23% year over year, with outbound loads to the U.S. up 31%, while an equipment research firm put the Canadian tractor count 2.9% below a year earlier. Carriers have a little more leverage than they did in spring, and they know it.


What that means for you: on brokered freight, your fuel exposure lives in the gap between two surcharge programs. If you can't see that gap per load, you can't defend it.


So by lunch you have three problems: a lagging index, a national price on regional lanes, and a tax calendar nobody priced. Time to decide.


## 1:30 p.m.: what you actually decide


You don't send the shipper a discount. You send her a better program. Here's the checklist you work through.


**Index and timing**


-


Switch to a weekly published index (NRCan's weekly average) for the region where your trucks actually fuel, not the national figure. Ontario lanes can use the province's weekly survey.


-


Update weekly, in both directions. A table that falls when diesel falls is the one that earns trust when diesel jumps again.


-


Write the index name, the publication day and the effective day into the contract, so nobody argues about which number counts.


**Base and math**


-


Reset the base price. If nobody can explain it, it's a negotiating weakness.


-


Show the math in fuel-efficiency terms both sides understand, such as litres per 100 km and a per-kilometre surcharge, alongside the percentage.


**Tax dates**


-


Add a clause that names the scheduled tax changes: January 1 (Alberta's earliest restart), January 31 (PEI), and February 1 and April 1 (federal excise).


-


Agree now that scheduled tax changes flow through the index automatically, so January doesn't become a second renegotiation.


**Brokerage side**


-


Price carrier fuel and customer fuel off the same index and update day wherever you can.


-


Where you can't, track the fuel spread per load as its own line, so margin from timing is visible and defensible.


**Accruals**


-


Accrue IFTA by jurisdiction monthly instead of discovering the bill each quarter. Western fuel savings should be booked net of the tax you'll owe elsewhere.


Your reply to the procurement lead goes out at 3 p.m. It accepts weekly updates starting December 1, proposes a regional index, and flags the 2027 tax dates with the expected per-kilometre effect of each.


She replies in 40 minutes: "This is the first fuel proposal I can actually explain to my CFO."


## Why the table has to fit your network


Here's what the fall of 2026 taught: two carriers on the same index can have completely different fuel exposure.


A Quebec-heavy regional fleet and an Alberta-based cross-border carrier don't buy the same diesel or owe the same tax. A broker running all-in rates has a different problem from a dedicated fleet with a contracted program. One-size fuel tables were always a compromise. At $2.75 diesel, the compromise got too expensive to ignore.


That's why serious shops build fuel rules into their systems, not their spreadsheets. Effective-dated surcharge schedules per customer. A regional index assigned per lane. Carrier-side and customer-side fuel tracked on every load. A tax calendar that alerts pricing before January 1, not after the first invoice dispute. Permissions so a rep can't override a surcharge without a note.


None of that is exotic. It's just your business, written down where it can't drift.


The next jump will come. Refining margins are still far above last year, inventories are thin, and winter heating demand is ahead. When it arrives, you want a table that already moves every week, already knows its index, and already knows what January brings.


The shipper's email will come again too. Next time, you'll want to answer it in five minutes.


## Frequently asked questions


### Why is Canadian diesel still so expensive if prices are falling?


Diesel is still expensive mostly because refining margins remain very high. NRCan estimated the refining margin in Vancouver's diesel price at 138.8 cents a litre in late November 2026, against 86.6 cents a year earlier, because global diesel inventories are still thin after the Middle East and Russian supply disruptions.


### When do Canadian fuel taxes on diesel come back?


Several return in early 2027. Alberta's 13-cent fuel tax is paused until at least December 31, 2026, and can restart from January 1 at no more than 9 cents per quarter. PEI's 14.15-cent diesel tax is zero through January 31, 2027. The federal 4-cent excise tax returns at 2 cents on February 1 and 4 cents on April 1, 2027.


### Should my fuel surcharge use the national average or a regional index?


Use a regional index whenever your lanes are concentrated in one area. Pump prices in November 2026 ranged from about $1.91 a litre in Edmonton to $2.54 in Laval on one fleet's fuel card, so a national average overpays on some lanes and underpays on others.


### Does buying cheaper diesel in Alberta lower my fuel tax?


No, not for interprovincial carriers. Under IFTA, fuel tax is owed where the kilometres are driven, so tax saved at an Alberta pump is settled on your quarterly return for the provinces you actually run through. Only the pre-tax price difference is a true saving.


### How often should a fuel surcharge update in a volatile market?


Weekly is the practical standard in a volatile market. Ontario's weekly fuel survey rose about 16 cents a litre in a single week in September 2026, so a monthly table can fall weeks behind, which hurts carriers when prices rise and shippers when they fall.
